Representative_Docs: [' The Ontario government is making a major move in support of journalism in the province. Premier Doug Ford has instructed his ministers that as of September, a significant portion of the province\'s advertising budget must be spent with Ontario media outlets. Perhaps more importantly, Ford has instructed his ministers in charge of the province\'s four biggest agencies, in terms of advertising, to do the same. Letters have now been sent to the chairs of the Ontario Lottery and Gaming Commission, the Liquor Control Board of Ontario, Metrolinx, and the Ontario Cannabis Store. Starting later this summer, each of these agencies will be required to set aside 25% of their advertising budget for provincially based sources."Ontario\'s major government agencies are some of the largest advertisers in the province, together spending well over $100 million on marketing each year," the letters state. "These significant advertising budgets should help support Ontario-based publishers and the Ontario-based workers creating local news content for people in our province."In the letters to the organizations, the Ford government states that they want the Crown agencies to spend more advertising with "Ontario-based corporations, trusts or partnerships that have been designated as Qualified Canadian Journalism Organizations by the Canada Revenue Agency."The list of organizations qualified by the federal government includes small and large publications including titles owned by Postmedia, owner of the Toronto Sun as well as other such newspapers as the National Post, London Free Press and Ottawa Citizen. Community publications such as The Creemore Echo or specialized publications such as The Trillium newsletter covering Queen\'s Park also qualify. Governments of all stripes and at all levels across the country have said that they want to support journalism, but few have been willing to do so, putting most of their money into Google and Facebook products. The latest annual report from the federal government shows that they spent $1.1 million advertising on TikTok in fiscal year 2022-23 despite all the security concerns around the social media app which has been banned from government devices. By comparison, the Trudeau government spent just $944,602 on any and all print advertising across Canada in the same year. TikTok received more advertising from the federal government that fiscal year than every Postmedia newspaper, the Toronto Star, the Globe and Mail, Journal de Montreal and every community newspaper combined. It\'s an odd message for the federal government to send to the media industry, saying that we are vital for news organizations\'future but we\'re just going to spend all of our advertising with digital giants. The federal government, which currently spends 71% of their advertising budget on digital, should consider a similar move to what Ford is pushing through. It would be a far better way to support journalism and homegrown media outlets that giving all your money to Facebook and Google while sending subsidy cheques to media companies. In the latest federal advertising report, $9.9 million is spent on search engine marketing, the same amount the government spent on all television advertising across Canada. The bulk of that money goes to Google, while most of the $13 million the feds spend on social media marketing goes to Meta, the parent company of Facebook and Instagram. In the most recent Review of Government Advertising by the auditor general for the province of Ontario, $4.5 million out of $28.8 million of Ontario government ad spending went to print advertising. That works out to roughly 16% of all reviewable Ontario government ads. While the directive letters are aimed at the four main agencies and their advertising budgets, the Ford government will go further and require the same 25% of all government advertising spending be placed with Ontario publishers."When in place across Ontario\'s major agencies, this new initiative promises to flow over $25 million to Ontario-based publishers, helping to protect jobs and promote local content and culture," Finance Minister Peter Bethlenfalvy wrote to LCBO Chair Carmine Nigro."The Government of Ontario is making similar commitments with our own advertising spending, helping to provide even more support for Ontario jobs and promote Ontario culture."Canada\'s media industry has gone through incredible upheaval over the past decade or more. That said, there is still an audience for news that informs us what is happening in our country, our province and our hometowns with a local point of view. You don\'t get that by spending your entire advertising budget with organizations based in Menlo Park or Mountain View, California. You get that by supporting quality local journalism by advertising with the publishers making the investment in your own community. Premier Doug Ford\'s bold move is not only a welcome one, it\'s also a move that should be emulated by Prime Minister Justin Trudeau across the federal government and by provincial and municipal governments across the country. blilley@postmedia.com @brianlilley', ' The Ontario government is making a major move in support of journalism in the province. Postmedia News blilley@postmedia.com', ' Ontario\'s Ford government will direct one-quarter of its advertising budget toward news publishers in Canada\'s largest province, a targeted boost for a major domestic industry facing unprecedented pressure from internationally owned technology giants. That should amount to about $25 million in advertising each year going to Ontario publishers, including Postmedia Network Inc., which owns National Post, the Toronto Sun, Ottawa Citizen and community papers in the province."This is important. Everyone understands the value of journalism and a free press and its criticality to Canada and to democracy," said Andrew MacLeod, Postmedia\'s president and chief executive officer."I\'m certainly extremely grateful to the leadership of Premier (Doug) Ford and his team. My hope is this will serve as an example, a North Star, not just for other provincial governments, but for the federal government and for major corporations."In a letter, sent to Metrolinx (the public transit Crown corporation), the Ontario Lottery Gaming Corporation, the Ontario Cannabis Retail Corporation and the Liquor Control Board of Ontario, Ontario Finance Minister Peter Bethlenfalvy asks the government agencies to have the policy implemented by Sept. 3."Our government believes strongly in the importance of supporting and promoting Ontariomade products, services and workers," Bethlenfalvy\'s letter says. The initiative is in addition to the Progressive Conservative government\'s Building Ontario Businesses Initiative, which uses government procurement spending to support Ontario businesses, the Ontario Made Manufacturing Investment Tax Credit and initiatives aimed at boosting sales of Ontario-made beer and wine. Supporting workers"In addition to these actions, we believe there\'s a compelling opportunity to leverage the advertising spends of Ontario\'s major government agencies to support Ontario workers and content," the letter says. Ontario\'s major government agencies spend more than $100 million each year on advertising."These significant advertising budgets should help support Ontario-based publishers and the Ontario-based workers creating local news content for people in our province," the letter says. Publications eligible for the government advertising must be designated "Qualified Canadian Journalism Organizations" by the federal Canada Revenue Agency and must be Ontario-based corporations, trusts or partnerships."The Government of Ontario is making similar commitments with our own advertising spending, helping to provide even more support for Ontario jobs and promote Ontario culture," the letter says. MacLeod said the initiative is something the publishing industry has been lobbying for with the Ontario government and other governments in Canada, including the federal government, and that it "didn\'t make sense" that advertising dollars, paid for by taxpayers, were going to Google and Facebook."As I\'ve said countless times, the single biggest challenge facing our industry is that 90 per cent of the digital advertising budgets flow to foreign platforms," MacLeod said. "This is the first major, material step where we\'re seeing a significant institution, the province of Ontario, allocating a material portion of their spend on Ontario publishers, which supports Ontario journalism, Ontario jobs and the Ontario economy."Companies, including Postmedia, will need to wait to figure out just how much money they could get and what it will mean, MacLeod said."It\'s a hugely meaningful moment for our industry, certainly from an Ontario perspective, and to the extent that it serves as a beacon or a catalyst for other provincial governments and for the federal government to do the same," MacLeod said."What does it mean for Postmedia? I think time will tell. But we\'re one of the larger players, and we should have a meaningful pro rata portion of that based on the audiences that we reach in Ontario."The directive will be reviewed quarterly, the letter says. If it is not working to meet the objectives of "promoting local content and culture and supporting Ontario jobs," the government notes it may withdraw the funding directive. Postmedia, the largest newspaper company in Canada, saw its revenues drop to $97.3 million for the three-month period ending Feb. 29, 2024. It was mostly attributable to a 20.8% fall in advertising revenue.']

Representative_Docs: [' And they\'re off. Doug Ford plunged Ontario into a Feb. 27 election on Tuesday, more than a year early in a bid for a third majority government. Ford met with Lt.-Gov. Edith Dumont to request the dissolution of the legislature, setting the stage for a 29-day campaign officially beginning Wednesday. It will be the first winter provincial vote since 1981.Ford is rushing Ontarians to the polls amid political instability in Ottawa after Prime Minister Justin Trudeau announced that he would resign and economic uncertainty over U.S. President Donald Trump\'s threat of 25 per cent tariffs on Canadian goods."This is going to be a battle for the next four years, and I want to make sure that I have an make sure I have a strong mandate to outlast President Trump," Ford told reporters at Queen\'s Park before his ceremonial visit to Dumont. Doug Ford has strong support as election call looms, survey suggestsThe Progressive Conservative leader will formally launch his campaign in Windsor on Wednesday against the backdrop of the Detroit skyline. That\'s to underscore that his rationale for the snap vote is to get a renewed mandate to deal with hefty levies on Canadian exports that Trump is threatening to begin this Saturday. But Ford, who is well ahead of his rivals in public-opinion surveys, has been scrambling for a reason to go early since last May. NDP Leader Marit Stiles, Liberal Leader Bonnie Crombie and Green Leader Mike Schreiner argue he\'s opportunistically trying to get in front of potential fallout from the RCMP\'s ongoing criminal investigation into the $8.28-billion Greenbelt land swap scandal. As first disclosed by the Star, the Mounties have interviewed past and current Ford staffers as part of their probe, and sources say the detectives\' work is continuing during the writ period. The opposition leaders would prefer Ford focus on the trade war with the U.S. and wait for the scheduled June 2026 vote instead of triggering an "unnecessary election" that will cost between $150 million and $175 million."While the people of Ontario are anxious about the grave threat of tariffs, Doug Ford is pursuing his own political gain," said Stiles."People need a premier who will fight like hell for every single job that\'s at risk, not run to the polls over a year early. Doug Ford thinks that he can call an early election to escape his record of failure on housing, health care, education and affordability. We won\'t let him," she said. Crombie accused Ford of "wasting $175 million on an early election instead of using it to fix our broken health-care system and make your life more affordable."Doug Ford\'s Ontario has failed you. I\'ll deliver more for you by guaranteeing you\'ll have a family doctor, cutting taxes on your paycheque and home heating and building homes you can afford," she said. Schreiner pointed to Ford\'s failure to deliver on housing."He\'s had seven years with a majority government to do something about it and the problem has only gotten worse," said the Green leader."It\'s time to kick out this NIMBY government and elect a government that will urgently build the homes we need to address the housing crisis."Ford\'s rivals also contend his efforts should also be spent tackling Ontario\'s doctor shortage instead of electioneering. But the Tory leader insisted he needs a new mandate because any Trump tariffs could necessitate tens of billions of dollars in stimulus spending to keep the economy afloat and people employed. Stiles, Crombie and Schreiner say they would back any such emergency expenditures. As chair of the Council of the Federation, Ford has aligned himself with Trudeau, forcefully making the case that Canada must retaliate with counter-tariffs against the U.S.Labour leaders urge Doug Ford to forgo an election and focus on Trump\'s tariff threatHis campaign maintains the election timing has to do with that and not the Greenbelt scandal stemming from him granting permission for developers to build on 7,400 acres of environmentally sensitive land. He reversed that decision after damning reports in August 2023 from the auditor general and the integrity commissioner revealed wealthy landowners with ties to the Tories had been "favoured."Despite his September 2023 U-turn to thwart the development plans, the Mounties swept in the following month and about a dozen of his current and former aides have been interviewed. Ford, maintaining his government has "nothing to hide" on the Greenbelt, set the table for a snap campaign with voter-friendly $200 "rebate" cheques that are now being mailed out to 15 million Ontario adults and children. That $3-billion payout is designed to offset Ontarians\' affordability concerns at a time of rising prices and unemployment rates creeping up. He also spent an additional $612 million to expedite the liberalization of booze sales so beer, wine and premixed cocktails could be sold in all supermarkets, corner stores and big box outlets in time for the snap election. In keeping with his populist bent and a penchant for intervening on matters traditionally the purview of municipalities, Ford announced portions of existing bike lanes on Bloor Street West in Etobicoke and University Avenue and Yonge Street in downtown Toronto would be removed to help alleviate the city\'s chronic gridlock. Mindful that the $6.2-million Transportation Tomorrow Survey found 3.1 per cent of Toronto residents commute to work by bicycle each morning - and 3.6 per cent use their bikes "all day" in a city of three million people where 164,806 daily cycling trips are made - the Tories believe curbing some bike lanes could be popular with voters who drive. Similarly, Ford is closing most supervised drug injection sites by forcing them to locate at least 200 metres away from schools and daycares while boosting provincial supports for addiction treatment as of March 31.While that change was criticized by some health advocates, who predict more overdoses, it was hailed by some Toronto residents who are fed up with drug dealers. Among the sites closing is one in Leslieville\'s South Riverdale Community Health Centre, near where mother-of-two Karolina Huebner-Makurat was killed by a stray bullet in July 2023, a brazen daylight crime that shocked the city. As the legislature rose Dec. 12 for the winter break, Ford announced new measures to address the homeless tent encampments that have sprung up in parks across Toronto and throughout the province, promising an additional $75.5 million for shelters and affordable housing - and toughening up trespassing laws. Since he took office almost seven years ago, the housing shortage has increased in fast-growing Ontario and there are now an estimated 81,000 homeless people in the province. After his Tories won power in 2018, ending an almost 15-year Liberal dynasty under premiers Kathleen Wynne and Dalton McGuinty, Ford was re-elected in 2022 following a global COVID-19 pandemic in which Ontario fared better than any neighbouring province or American state during the health emergency. Despite his current standing in the polls, not all PC operatives are happy about a snap election. They are concerned about history repeating itself, recalling that in 1990, popular Liberal premier David Peterson held an election a year early and was punished by voters, losing to Bob Rae\'s New Democrats in one of the largest upsets in Canadian political history. Peterson is now chair of Torstar, the Star\'s parent company. Along with that precedent, some Ford loyalists worry about the "Underhill balance theory," which posits that when Ontarians elect Liberals federally, they tend to choose Tories provincially. Conversely, when they elect federal Tory governments, the Liberals - and, once, in Rae\'s case, the NDP - usually win provincially at Queen\'s Park. With polls suggesting federal Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre will triumph in a national election expected later this year, the "balance" phenomenon was another consideration in going to provincial voters early. At dissolution, there were 79 Tories, including Speaker Ted Arnott, who is not seeking re-election, 28 New Democrats, nine Liberals, six Independents and two Greens in the 124-member house.', ' Good morning. I’m Abigale Subdhan, an audience editor at The Globe and Mail. Ontario Premier Doug Ford has confirmed he will launch a snap provincial election campaign this week, which would send voters to the polls on Feb. 27. More on what we know so far, plus a peek at a thriving punk scene in Saint John and what else to expect this week. But first:Today’s headlines- The Israel-Hamas ceasefire is under strain as Trump proposes emptying Gaza of Palestinians- The White House says Colombia agrees to take deported migrants after Trump’s tariff showdown- Holocaust survivors share the lessons that must never be forgotten- Kansas City will go up against Philadelphia in a quest for their third straight Super Bowl titleOntario politics Doug Ford confirms early election call There has been speculation for months that Ford was preparing to call an early election. Last week, while speaking to reporters at an event in Brampton, Ont., he definitively ended the speculation and said he was taking the province to the polls – just 2½ years after he won a majority in 2022.Queen’s Park reporter Jeff Grey took the time to answer our question about what Ontarians can expect with a four-week election cycle. Here’s what he had to say. How did we get here?There have been many months of this kind of speculation – and it was thought it would be in the spring. Turns out, it’s going to be in the depths of cold February. More recently, with the election of Donald Trump and the announcement of potential 25-per-cent tariffs on Canadian goods, which will hit Ontario and its manufacturing industry extremely hard, the Premier – who has emerged as the de facto spokesman for Canada in dealing with the threat from Washington – has said he needs a new mandate from Ontario voters to take on four more years of Trump. It had become the question everyone asked every time he poked his face in front of the microphone, and he finally confirmed that Ontario will go to the polls. The campaign will start on Wednesday, Jan. 29, and we’ll vote on Thursday, Feb. 27.Why is Doug Ford calling an election right now?Before we got into this Trump tariff crisis, the strategies around calling an early election revolved around a desire to get ahead of any future federal election, and there are a couple reasons why Ford would want to do that. One, Ontario voters historically vote for the other party. So if there is an election at Queen’s Park, Ontarians tend to vote for whoever’s not in power in Ottawa – and vice versa. So the Progressive Conservative Party of Ontario likely wanted to get ahead of that dynamic, possibly. They were also concerned that a new Conservative government in Ottawa, as all polls suggest we’re going to have, will cut spending and cut the money that is sent to provinces – and that would complicate Doug Ford’s life, because he doesn’t want to cut spending. There is also the idea that he needs to get ahead of what could be a souring economy. What is the opposition saying about the move?The Premier’s main opponents – Official Opposition NDP Leader Marit Stiles and Liberal Leader Bonnie Crombie – have both charged that an early election is unnecessary. They say that instead of going out on the campaign trail, Ford should recall the legislature, now on an extended winter break, and focus on dealing with Trump’s threat. Interestingly, though, nobody seems ready. Nobody has candidates nominated in all 124 ridings yet, not even the governing party. As of last week, the PCs have somewhere in the range of 88 candidates nominated; the Liberals have around 70, and the NDP have somewhere just shy of 40 – and those numbers are changing all the time. The parties have also been scrambling to vet candidates, get nomination meetings going in order to get a full slate ready and raise money. Neither Stiles nor Crombie has faced a general election like this as leader, so this will be a new experience for both of them. What could the election campaign look like?One thing that will be weird about this election campaign is that Ford will spend three, four days in Washington talking to governors, senators, representatives and possibly the Trump administration to either get tariffs reversed or convince Trump to not tariff us at all. He’ll be tapping into that “Captain Canada” role he’s been in during the campaign, which is unusual. How do you think the campaign cycle will affect vulnerable Ontario workers?It’s impossible to game out what’s going to happen. If tariffs are announced on Feb. 1, how long does it take for companies to say, for example, we are shutting our factory in Ontario and opening one in Illinois? How fast do those kinds of adjustments happen? How many job losses happen right away? No one really knows. The other complicated thing is if the provincial government is going to spend a ton of money to help Ontario workers and businesses, they would normally need the legislature to approve the ask. But the legislature has been dissolved and can’t meet until elections are over – which is a whole month or more, until Feb. 27.What could be other major hot topics in this election?', ' Premier Doug Ford is sending voters to the polls 15 months early, with a snap election he says is needed to deal with the threat posed to Ontario\'s economy by U.S. President Donald Trump and his avowed tariffs on Canadian exports. Here are some key things to know ahead of Wednesday\'s expected election call: BLAMING TRUMP Even before Trump took office this month, Ford - with two majority Progressive Conservative governments under his belt - appeared to be itching for an early election. Speculation about an election before the next scheduled one, in June 2026, ran rampant last fall as Ford ruled out a late 2024 vote but refused to take 2025 off the table. Then came Trump\'s election in November and his inauguration in January, with his threat to slap 25 per cent tariffs on Canadian exports to the U.S. Such a move could cost up to 500,000 jobs in Ontario\'s export-driven economy, some officials estimate."Make no mistake about it, he\'s coming for us," the premier has warned. Ford, who has become something of a Captain Canada in recent weeks, appearing widely in American media to defend Canadian interests amid the Trump threat, now insists he needs a "clear mandate" to deal with four years of Trump\'s second presidency and the damaging fallout it could have on Ontario. CRITICS SEE CYNICISM Critics contend Ford doesn\'t need to call an early election, since he has a majority government and as premier already has the job of defending Ontario\'s interests."While our province faces a grave threat with half a million jobs at risk, Doug Ford sees an opportunity to fight for one job - his own," New Democrat leader Marit Stiles, the opposition leader at Queen\'s Park, said Friday."He thinks he can con Ontarians with an early election to escape his record - but we won\'t let him."Wednesday\'s election-call will come nearly two weeks after Ontario started mailing out $200 cheques to virtually every man, woman and child in the province, a roughly $3-billion mass mail-out of money that Ford promised last fall to help Ontarians cope with higher costs including from the federal Liberal carbon tax. Opponents have categorized the move as an attempt to buy voters with their own money. Ford\'s PCs have a commanding majority in the Ontario legislature, holding about two-thirds of its seats."It does seem opportunistic. Like many people, I suspect, I\'m skeptical of the rationale of needing a new mandate," said Matt Farrell, a political science instructor at Fanshawe College in London."What more of a mandate does he need? He has a 50-seat lead in the legislature now."WHAT \'S NEXT - Coming off a "super-caucus" strategy meeting with PC candidates Saturday, Ford will visit Ontario\'s lieutenant-governor on Wednesday to ask that the legislature be dissolved and the election writs issued, one for each riding in the province. That will trigger a 29-day campaign, with the election held Feb. 27 - one month after Trump has hinted his avowed tariffs could take effect, and 10 days before the federal Liberals choose a new leader for their fragile minority government to replace the departing Justin Trudeau as prime minister. A federal election is widely expected to follow soon after, with either the Liberal government falling sometime after the prorogued Parliament resumes March 24 or the new prime minister pulling the plug and sending voters to the polls. HISTORY ON THE LINE Ford is gunning for a third straight majority under his watch, something no Ontario premier has pulled off since 1959. Liberal premier Dalton McGuinty came oh-so close in 2011, finishing the election that year one seat shy of three straight majorities. Between them, John Robarts and Bill Davis managed three consecutive PC majorities ending in 1971. But for the last majority hat trick under one premier, you have to go back to Leslie Frost who led his PCs to victory in 1951, \'55 and \'59.THE MAGIC NUMBERS Ford\'s PCs hold 79 seats in the 124-seat legislature, the opposition NDP 28 and the Liberals nine. The Green party has two seats and six members sit as independents. A party needs to win 63 seats for a simple majority, but more is better since the speaker of the legislature usually comes from the ruling party, reducing its voting strength by one. THE COST Another important number to consider? The actual cost of sending Ontarians to the polls. The province\'s last general election in 2022 cost taxpayers $145.3 million, but the tab is expected to be higher this time factoring in increased costs and the run-up in inflation since then. THE ISSUES Ford is trying to frame the election as a referendum on which leader and party is best suited to deal with Trump and the billions of dollars the U.S. president\'s avowed tariffs could cost Ontario. Watch for the other parties to zero in on government baggage ranging from homelessness and the affordability crisis many Ontarians are feeling, the 2.5 million residents of the province with no family doctor and a criminal investigation by the RCMP into a controversial plan to remove land for new housing from the protected Greenbelt near Toronto, a land swap the Tories moved to reverse following a public and political uproar. Heading into the election, a Leger poll conducted for Postmedia and published last week suggested affordability concerns are the top issue, with 28 per cent of respondents ranking the cost of living as the most important issue in their community. That was far ahead of the No. 2 issue, health care, at 12 per cent, and the economy, which was a top priority for 11 per cent. Five per cent ranked U.S. relations, including Trump tariffs, as the most important issue. AREN\'T ELECTION DATES FIXED? Yes and no. Ontario has a fixeddate election law, requiring one to be held every four years, but that doesn\'t stop the lieutenant-governor from dissolving the legislature at the request of the premier. Under the law, Ontario\'s next election date would have been June 4, 2026.THE RISK The last time an Ontario premier with a majority called an early election, it backfired badly. Liberal premier David Peterson, high in the polls three years into a majority, called an election in 1990 with economic storm clouds on the horizon. What looked to be a summer sleeper for the Liberals quickly turned into a nightmare. Beset by single-issue protest groups and suspicion the Liberals were trying to bag another victory before tough times hit, the party lost the election - and Peterson his London seat - to Bob Rae\'s New Democrats, who battled a brutal recession that followed. There\'s always a risk voters could punish Ford for the early election, returning his government in a weakened position, said Laura Stephenson, chair of the political science department at Western University. THE REWARD While there\'s always a risk in ending an otherwise stable majority, Farrell said the potential payoff for Ford outweighs the dangers. Calling an election now means Ford can catch the Liberals, under leader Bonnie Crombie, at a time when they\'re still rebuilding from severe election defeats in 2018 and 2022, Farrell said."The new Liberal leader has not really been defined yet for voters," he said. "It gives the PCs a chance to define the Liberal leader while being in a position of strength as an incumbent government."This election will be the first as party leader for both Crombie, who took the Liberal helm in December 2023, and for the NDP\'s Stiles, who took over from Andrea Horwath in February 2023.Even though federal and provincial politics are separate, the recent turmoil for Trudeau\'s Liberals could also affect how some voters see the Ontario Liberals, Farrell said. THE HORSE RACE Recent polling suggests Ford\'s PCs enter the starting gate with the election theirs to lose. The latest Leger survey of voter intentions, conducted Jan. 17 to 19, found Ford\'s PCs with the support of 46 per cent of respondents, to 22 per cent for Crombie\'s Liberals. When asked who they\'d vote for if an election was held today, 19 per cent of respondents said they\'d vote for the NDP. The survey results are considered accurate to within 3.08 per cent, plus or minus, 19 times out of 20. jbieman@postmedia.com']

Representative_Docs: [' I graduated from medicine at the University of Toronto in 1971, three years after the inception of Medicare in Canada in 1968.As soon as government took total control for paying them, suddenly there were too many doctors doing too many operations, generating too many visits, making too much money. The medical profession, the College of Physicians and Surgeons, the Ontario Medical Association, have absolutely no influence on medical manpower numbers -it is the provincial government that has absolute control. For the last 55 years, provincial governments have tried to cut health-care spending by limiting the number of doctors, clawing back their fees, capping their incomes and limiting the number of billing numbers (which are needed for a doctor to be paid).The Ontario government decides how many doctors it wants to pay and limits medical school enrolments accordingly. Despite crippling physician shortages, each provincial government still imposes tight quotas on how many students are allowed to enrol at the country\'s 17 medical schools, a "choke point" that limits student admissions to just under 2,900 spots for prospective doctors each year. Ontario has six medical schools, all of which have acceptance rates of less than 10 per cent, four below five per cent. As long as the government is the sole single payer for physician services, it will be the choke point for physician numbers and the reason for the doctor shortage. The shortage of doctors is the fault of every Ontario provincial government regardless of party, not just Doug Ford\'s Progressive Conservatives. And up to now, governments have been fine with that; all three main political parties, and every premier in every Ontario government since the inception of Medicare. Bob Rae\'s NDP government, 1990-1995, slashed medical school enrolment in Ontario by 10 per cent in 1993 and the repercussions are still felt today..The Bob Rae NDP government of 1990-1995 in Ontario implemented the Barer-Stoddart report, which postulated that hordes of surplus medical school graduates were going to suck the system dry by generating scads of unnecessary medical encounters. In one bizarre example of top-down central planning run amok, the Rae government announced it would pay the University of Toronto up to $10 million a year to not produce as many doctors. Zealous politicians in many provinces offered incentives for physicians to retire early or contemplated other methods to reduce physician supply, such as limiting billing numbers and capping physician incomes. Not long ago, Ontario wouldn\'t allow new doctors except in "underserviced" areas, such as Sioux Lookout, which medical students in Toronto always confuse with Sault Ste Marie. Quebec currently does the same thing, forcing new graduates to work in the boondocks if they want to be paid by the province\'s healthcare plan. Which is why so many family doctors in Montreal and Quebec City have opted out of the public system completely and are private. The Mike Harris Progressive Conservative government that followed Rae pushed tax reductions and slashed public spending on health care, closed hospitals, privatized long-term care and eliminated the jobs of thousands of nurses, infamously comparing them to obsolete hula hoop makers. In 1996, Harris announced a 10 per cent "clawback" in the fees paid to Ontario doctors for services they provide, the first of several. The fee schedule has never been unclawed and today the present Ontario fee schedule is 70 per cent lower than the fee schedule of the Ontario Medical Association for uninsured patients..In 1997 Harris capped physician incomes and declared that doctors who cut back on the number of patients they see because they\'ve hit their billing caps should lose their medical licences -all this while there was a physician shortage. Kathleen Wynne\'s Liberal government, 2013-2018, went to war with physicians in the mid 2010s. On Feb. 1 2015, rather than opt for a fair, binding arbitration process, the Liberal government proceeded to unilaterally impose a 2.65 per cent cut to all doctor services (on top of the 2.5 per cent cut from 2012) and an arbitrary cap on total compensation to doctors. Without a doubt, family physicians were the most heavily impacted physicians. This meant that once patients\'demand for care exceeded the allocated $12 billion, the doctors themselves were responsible for subsidizing the difference through a further claw-back. Any other profession would go on strike, but doctors realize how much our patients need us, and we would never go on strike (nor are we allowed to by our regulatory college).The only recourse doctors had was to retire or to leave the province. Which many did. The Wynne government thought it was a good idea to cut 50 residency positions (training for doctors) and only saw the light during a deathbed confession just in time for the 2018 election. The Ontario government\'s contempt for family physicians resulted in, as OMA vice-chair Audrey Karlinsky put it, a cohort of six years of medical graduates not choosing family medicine when hundreds of thousands of people didn\'t have a family doctor. The decision of former premier Kathleen Wynne\'s Liberal government to cut 50 medical residency positions in Ontario over two years was done for one reason only. That was to save money by cutting the number of doctors in a province that desperately needed them, playing on the politics of envy, painting doctors as fat cats, a tactic government uses over and over again. Canada spends less of its total health budget on primary care than the average among Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD) countries (5.3 per cent vs. 8.1 per cent).At the same time, Canada is seeing declining enrolment in family medicine as a specialty among medical students, and more graduating family physicians are choosing not to practise generalist office-based care, opting instead for being hospitalists or ER doctors. No one wants to be a family doctor. With good reasons. The number of Ontarians without a family doctor, as of Sept. 2022, has surpassed 2.3 million (up from 1.8 million in 2020), over 14.8 per cent of all Ontarians according to a new report. The Ontario College of Family Physicians\'latest forecast is that approximately one in four Ontarians - that\'s 4.4 million - will be without a family doctor by 2026.To make up for that shortfall, and without even considering physicians on the cusp of retirement, Ontario would need approximately 1,700 new family doctors. A retrospective study of community-dwelling seniors who were admitted to Thunder Bay Regional Health Sciences Centre examined the association between family physician status and outcomes among those with a family physician. Among the 12,033 seniors admitted to hospital between 2004, and 2013, 40.7 per cent lacked a family physician. There was a 60 per cent higher chance of dying while in hospital plus a 21 per cent higher chance of dying in the year afterwards for those with no family doctor. The health-care system is complicated and a family doctor is vital in navigating the system. Canada can learn from OECD countries such as the Netherlands, Norway, the UK and Finland, where more than 95 per cent of people have a primary care clinician, near-universal insurance coverage exists, the proportion of health spending that is spent on primary care is larger than Canada\'s and GPs are organized better in teams and are more accountable for the care they must provide. Ten per cent of medical doctors in Finland work solely in the private sector. They also have a right to collect user fees set at a maximum of 46 Euros. The Netherlands offers mandatory insurance that is managed by private insurance companies and you pay a compulsory deductible for the first part of healthcare you receive under the insurance. In Norway, citizens are responsible for paying a certain amount in user fees until they reach a certain amount of money paid outof-pocket, when they receive an exemption card for public health services, and no longer have to pay user fees for the remainder of the calendar year. Allow patients to pay for private care if they so choose. Sweden, Finland, Germany, Australia, Denmark, Japan, Germany - basically every other rich developed country with a universal health-care system allows this option and has better outcomes than Canada. When access to timely care cannot be provided in the publicly funded system, Canadians should be able to use private health insurance to reimburse the cost of care obtained in the private sector rather than die waiting. Since 2013, there have been 931 patients who died in Ontario while waiting for heart surgery longer than the maximum recommended wait time. Then there are those who die while waiting for scans or surgeries that would have improved their quality of life, like a hip operation. Over 17,000 Canadians died while waiting for surgery or a diagnostic scan in 2022-23.Universal public healthcare is a right but one should have the option of accessing better (often more costly, more advanced medical technology such as laser cataract surgery not available on OHIP), faster, more timely care if so desired, as everyone in every other modern, industrialized wealthy country in the world can. This approach helps reduce wait times every time a patient decides to pay for private care. Shaking up the way hospitals are funded could also help. Hospitals severely limit OR time because more surgeries are seen as a cost coming out of a pre-determined global budget. Fund more OR time, reward hospitals for being more productive, shortening patient wait times. Instead of giving hospitals a large cheque at the beginning of the year and hoping for the best, governments could pay them based on their performance and output. Health-care is a right, not a privilege, but like food and shelter, it is also a commodity. We do not mandate that everyone eat Hamburger Helper or live in row housing. Political ideology run amok has elevated government single-payer one-tier health care to an impossible pedestal. Clinging to an ideology of government single-payer one-tier health-care is simply misguided virtue-signalling on a national scale. Should we be proud of a health-care system where governments abandon patients to die? And make no mistake, people will die because of not having a family doctor. Obviously not. These international examples can inform bold policy reform in Canada to advance a vision of primary care for all.', ' KINGSTON-The sprawling second-floor office, located above a pharmacy on the city\'s main street, at one time was home to eight doctors serving the busy neighbourhood. But the physicians, with large patient rosters, were burning out and six were ready to retire, but couldn\'t find anyone willing to take over the practice. Two years ago, they all left, the clinic shuttered and 8,000 patients suddenly found themselves adrift - joining about two million others across the province with no access to a family doctor. It\'s not a problem unique to Kingston - many communities across the province are grappling with a lack of primary care - and it has emerged as a key issue in Ontario\'s Feb. 27 election. The opposition parties have hammered the PCs for being in power for seven years as the situation they inherited worsened, which even the government acknowledged has taken too long to fix and left too many without a family doctor. But what has happened here since that clinic closed is a new model that has been able to attract physicians and taken thousands off the wait-list, a model that appears to have the support of the PCs, Liberals and NDP.That same Princess Street office reopened last summer as a "primary care home," as proposed by Dr. Jane Philpott, a former federal Liberal health minister and dean of the medical school at Queen\'s recently hired by the PC government to help fix the province\'s health problems. Her vision, outlined in her 2024 book Health for All - which she calls the periwinkle model - guarantees primary care for everyone based on their postal code, much like families being assigned a local school based on their address. Two days before the provincial election campaign kicked off last week, the government and Philpott announced funding with a promise of primary care for all Ontarians by 2029, a total of $1.8 billion for every Ontarian to have a family doctor or primary care team within four years. The government, however, says two million Ontarians need a physician, which is based on work by organizations like the Canadian Institute for Health Information, but the Ontario Medical Association says the number is 2.5 million and could rise to 4.4 million by 2026.Last fall, Philpott spoke at the Liberal policy convention, and Leader Bonnie Crombie announced Thursday that if elected, she would spend $3 billion over four years to connect everyone with a family doctor. On Friday, NDP Leader Marit Stiles unveiled a $4.05 billion four-year plan to get all Ontarians access to a doctor or nurse practitioner, pledging more family health teams. Philpott\'s model, based on similar ones in the Netherlands and the United Kingdom, ideally provide patients access to care seven days a week, taking pressure of emergency rooms and steering them away from walk-in clinics. They are treated by practitioners they know, and who know their histories; medical records are in one place, and once a full network of sites are in place, no one would worry about finding a family doctor if they move. The Midtown Kingston Health Home opened last July, two years after a proposal by various health care partners in the city obtained funding from the provincial government. At the health home, each family doctor works in a team with a nurse practitioner, sharing "provider pod" offices, with a host of in-demand services on site - diabetes care, COPD care, social worker, family health educator - mostly for those within the K7M postal code. Community clinics for well baby care, sexual health and quick STI testing are open to all. Practical assistance workers help patients who might need help co-ordinating insulin injections for their child while at school, or finding housing, or applying for a birth certificate. It\'s hoping to secure funding to add occupational therapists, physiotherapists, mental health case management and footcare, to make it more of a one-stop community hub for patients."The doctors, they were asking me all kinds of questions about my history and this and that, and I was just blown away, because my (previous) doctor would not engage with anything you would have asked him, and I always felt rushed," said lifelong Kingston resident Mario Borsato, 56, now a patient of the health home. He and several of his family members had sought care at the original clinic for 20 years, and found themselves without a doctor for two years, so he knows the struggles of those who are still looking."If you don\'t have your health, you don\'t have nothing," he added. "And our family care (in the province) has gone down the tubes."About 4,400 residents in the K7M postal code were on the wait-list through Health Care Connect, but it is estimated the actual need is double that. So far, the health home has rostered 1,418 patients and - and treated another 1,535 through its various clinics - and expects to have 4,000 patients signed up by the end of March and 8,000 patients by March 2026.Winn Studsrud, a patient of the original clinic, was directed to the health home after seeking help with a prescription, but it wasn\'t until later that she realized she\'d been taken on by a family doctor there, even though she doesn\'t live in the postal code."I freaking started crying," she said. "I couldn\'t stop smiling, actually. And I just kept saying \'thank you Lord, thank you Lord.\' So honestly, it\'s like a miracle."Dr. Mary Rowland, clinical lead, calls the health home "a really nice blend" and likens it to a secondary school, where "this school has the IB program, this school has French Immersion. We have a catchment, and we have these specialized programs for more supports for particular populations."Dr. Eileen Nicolle, who moved with her family from Toronto to Kingston to be a part of the health home, said "you can provide the most holistic care and also take the time you need to see people ... I think if you take a more long-term approach, there\'s very much a cost saving and also a time saving because those problems that you don\'t deal with right up front, they come back."Currently, the clinic is open five days a week with evening clinic hours, and has managed to attract five physicians so far, with one to come, plus locums, as well as three nurse practitioners. Staff are on salary, have flexible hours and a team-centred approach. Doctors like it because they don\'t have to run a business as they would setting up their own practice. They work more reasonable hours, and can leave when they want, "but they don\'t" because it\'s such an attractive set up, said Meghan O\'Leary, director of clinical services for Kingston Community Health Centres. Nurse Practitioner Edward Cho was the first hire, and saw the patient roster grow - though initially there was some upset as those from the old clinic weren\'t necessarily able to re-register. Cho values being paired with a doctor, because "there are more opportunities for patients to get followups" in a timely manner."I\'m not worried about my patients" when away, he added. "I always know they\'re covered. If there are urgent issues, I know they\'re well taken care of ... having two eyes, rather than one, is always a good thing."Personally, he said the way the interdisciplinary model works gives him the "perfect work-life balance. I\'m not stressed. I go home knowing that my inbox is taken care of, and I won\'t come back to 10 million messages. I finish all my charting on time."For Nicolle, working with a male nurse practitioner gives patients choice. "Maybe they want to see a female for their Pap smear. Or maybe the men would rather see Ed for certain things. So it gives you a bit of diversity within the practice."Research on team-based care has been shown to benefit patients\' health and means a drop in hospitalizations and visits to the ER. Patients report higher levels of satisfaction and care, and health-care providers report higher job satisfaction and are less likely to burn out, says Jennifer Rayner, director of policy and research at the Alliance for Healthier Communities. Raisa Deber, professor emeritus at the Institute of Health Policy, Management and Evaluation at the University of Toronto, said there are a number of team-based models in the province, and there must be flexibility in the system because what works in a large, urban centre may not in a rural or remote area where it might be difficult to get additional services. Dr. Tara Kiran, family physician and researcher at St. Michael\'s Hospital and the University of Toronto, works in a family health team that includes nurses, nurse practitioners, social workers, pharmacists and others, focusing on a vulnerable population. When more than one in five people in Canada don\'t have access to any primary care, with services varying by region, "we need to do things differently to try and even out the way services are provided ... so that we don\'t have the have and have-not, but rather, everybody has something."The periwinkle model does address that and needs to be evaluated to see if it does attract doctors and is able to better clear wait-lists."There is a bit of an experiment here, and we do need to learn from it," Kiran added. The Kingston model is part of a wider network that has a community board of governors, which is key, said Kate Mulligan, a professor at the Dalla Lana School of Public Health at the University of Toronto."If we\'re going to go to all the trouble of doing team based primary care, which is the right next step, we shouldn\'t miss the opportunity to leverage the huge capacity that\'s there, to really connect that into our health care system," Mulligan said.', ' Retired family physician Marlene Spruyt, the Green Party candidate for Lanark-Frontenac-Kingston, remembers a time when she called up a home care nurse for a dying patient. "We delivered palliative care to a woman who was blind, and she got to stay at home and die," she says. "Now, you can\'t deliver that quality of care."For the 2.5 million Ontarians without a family doctor (up from 1.8 million in 2020), Spruyt\'s memory sounds like myth. But that level of care could return, if only leaders would summon up the political will. Ontarians are now being asked to choose a new leader. Progressive Conservative leader Doug Ford called a snap election for Feb. 27 in response to the threat of U.S. tariffs 16 months before an election was due. But according to a recent Nanos survey, nearly 30 per cent of voters say health care concerns will dictate how they cast their ballots. The Nanos poll shows 28 per cent of voters favour the Liberals on health care while 26 per cent support Ford. The NDP trails at 21 per cent. Perhaps most damning of all is the Nanos finding that one in five Ontarians don\'t trust any party on health care. Ontarians know just how precarious the health system is. For two decades, governments of all stripes have failed to address the demands of an exploding, aging population. The Ontario Medical Association predicts that by 2026 - that\'s next year - 4.4 million people won\'t have a family doctor. The OMA says Ontario needs 3,500 new family doctors now. It gets worse. Close to 40 per cent of family doctors are nearing retirement. Poor pay combined with runaway inflation make running the business of family practice financially unsustainable. The falling number of medical school seats per capita means a shortage of doctors coming down the pipeline. And that\'s just the family doctor crisis. The province also needs to fund new hospitals, maintain existing ones, and pay for seniors\' long-term care. Addressing health care is a gargantuan task, but Ford\'s majority government has had seven years to fix the mess. Last year, the Ministry of Health infuriated doctors by stating that the recruitment and retention of Ontario physicians was "not a major concern."In 2024, the federal government transferred $3.1 billion to Ontario for health care. Last fall, Ford recruited former federal Liberal health minister Jane Philpott to implement her Primary Care Action Plan. But this anemic, late-in-the-day proposal calls for just $1.8 billion to connect two million Ontarians to 305 vaguely defined primary care teams in a school-board type model based on residential postal codes. Her plan emphasizes workforce retention and easing administrative burden but is sketchy on financial details. It also adds 500 new medical school seats by 2028.The Greens, who boast only two MPPs, present a bolder platform. They say they\'ll recruit 3,500 family doctors. According to Marlene Spruyt, this plan represents a stark contrast from the PCs. Spruyt cites the various ways Ford has failed to shore up health care, including lost savings from breaking a contract with The Beer Store. For a guy who says he doesn\'t drink, she calls his beer fixation "bizarre.""What has Doug Ford done right?" she asks. Spruyt says municipalities shouldn\'t have to fund health care. She wants the government to pay half the cost to build hospitals in towns like Bracebridge, where rich donors are scarce. Nobody asks citizens to chip in for a new police car, she adds. For her part, NDP Leader Marit Stiles has pledged to spend $4 billion over four years to bring in 3,500 family doctors and 15,000 nurses to work in teams. The party\'s health critic France Gelinas represents the northern riding of Nickel Belt, where 30,000 residents lack a family doctor. She says the Ford government has knowingly allowed conditions to deteriorate, and adds that Ford\'s government listens to investors, while the NDP listens to front-line staff. Gelinas says the NDP respects family physicians."They\'ve been providing quality primary care for a very long time. They need to be paid fairly."She\'s also frustrated that although Sudbury\'s Northern Ontario School of Medicine can increase its capacity from 56 to 100 undergraduate seats "right now," the government won\'t release the funding yet. As for Bonnie Crombie\'s Liberals, they have also vowed to increase the number of physicians, promising to pair every Ontarian with a family doctor-led team of allied health professionals by spending $3.1 billion to "attract and retain 3,100 family doctors" by 2029. They will double medical school spots, entice 2,400 aging doctors to delay retirement and invest $250 million to recruit 650 doctors who\'ve decamped elsewhere for better pay and less paperwork back to family practice. Liberal Adil Shamji, the MPP for Don Valley East who, he says, is "the only elected physician" at Queen\'s Park says the government\'s track record speaks for itself, with lukewarm promises coming years too late. He says Ford found money for everything but health care, including $3.2 billion - which could pay for the Liberal health platform and then some - on $200 taxpayer rebates. Shamji says Ontarians pay taxes for family doctors and worries that to cut costs the current government is diluting the definition of primary care by trying to "convince Ontarians that if they have a pharmacist who can prescribe for minor ailments, that counts as ... primary care, and it doesn\'t."These juicy promises from political parties still trailing the incumbent in the polls sound like a Christmas wish list for patients and doctors alike. Adam Stewart, who practices comprehensive family medicine in Madoc, a rural town halfway between Toronto and Ottawa, believes that money is the priority. He sits on the board of the OMA\'s Section on General and Family Practice. Only 65 per cent of family doctors are left in comprehensive, longitudinal practices offering cradle to grave care. They\'re incurring "20, maybe 30 per cent increases" in overhead from post-pandemic inflation balanced against one per cent annual fee increases. Stewart says government needs to bump up family doctor compensation to be in line with BC and other provinces. He also wants Ontario to recognize family doctors as specialists in looking after patients from birth to death. They\'re ready to assume higher patient loads by leading multi-professional teams. Stewart also has some more unconventional recommendations. Put the joy back into medicine, he says, by providing doctors with AI technology for scribes. Implement a centralized referral system for rapid access to specialists and MRIs. These reforms are crucial, says Stewart. "If things don\'t get fixed," he says, if they continue down the same sad trajectory, he might have to leave comprehensive practice, too. Merrilee Fullerton, a retired family doctor and two-time Progressive Conservative MPP from Kanata-Carleton calls the Ford government\'s $1.8-billion offer "a hail Mary pass."Fullerton says too often, governments laud shiny baubles, like AI, that are distractions from the fact that family doctors are the glue that holds the system together. She resigned her seat in 2023 because of "tremendous frustration" with the government\'s lackadaisical approach to health care. Fullerton wants policymakers, bureaucrats, and politicians to think ahead. She calls making hasty health care election promises, then forgetting them till the next election cycle "irresponsible."In April 2005, faced with family doctor shortages, Liberal premier Dalton McGuinty announced new Family Health Teams to serve 2.5 million Ontarians. But when family doctors tried to join those teams, McGuinty and his successor Kathleen Wynne froze the funding. It was too expensive. Some lucky Ontarians got team-based care, while millions more didn\'t and even fewer do now. McGuinty also imposed the Health Premium tax in 2004, a levy of up to $900 that Ontarians still pay annually. There\'s nothing new here. Then, as now, Ottawa injected cash into Ontario\'s coffers. Then, as now, governments promised primary care teams to solve provincial health care woes. Will much-touted team funding be frozen again?Not one Ontario political party in the past 20 years has demonstrated the grit needed to fix health care. The Progressive Conservatives still lead the Liberals by 15 percentage points. Barring an electoral miracle, Ford seems destined to be a three-time premier. Patients are tired of not having family doctors to give their newborns their childhood shots, and are tired of waiting months to see the orthopedic surgeon while their knees crumble. Doctors are tired of working longer, harder, faster to keep their patients healthy with shrinking resources.']

Representative_Docs: [' Why is Doug Ford promising to send a $200 payment to every Ontarian? To put it bluntly, because he can. Ford made official what had been reported weeks ago that the fall economic statement will include a tax rebate - "Dougie Dollars" if you will."We\'re able to provide the relief because inflation has increased provincial sales tax revenues and because of the federal government\'s recent changes to their capital gains tax," Ford said. To give you an example of how inflation has increased the government\'s sales tax revenues, in fiscal year 2019-20, the first full year of the Ford government, sales tax revenue stood at $28.6 billion. In 2021-22, before inflation took off, that sales tax revenue had grown to $30.4 billion, but by the end of March the government was taking in $39.9 billion. That\'s an increase of 39.5% in four years just on the sales tax. Part of this is driven by inflation. Part of this is also driven by Ontario\'s incredible population growth. Ford said rather than hang onto the extra cash, he wants to give it back to taxpayers. Leaders of all three opposition parties at Queen\'s Park said that, rather than give the money back to taxpayers, Ford should be investing in health care or education. Ford said that his government can do both."It\'s not either/or keep costs down or invest in social programs, it\'s and. We can and are doing both," Ford said. Since he took office, health spending has increased 34.2% from $63.7 billion in 2019-20 to $85.5 billion in the last fiscal year and you can bet there will be increases announced Wednesday. Basically, the Ford government has more money than it can spend and rather than invent new programs, it\'s sending money back to you. A family of two parents and two kids will get $800 in Dougie Dollars by the end of January, just as Christmas credit card bills are coming due. You can call this crass electioneering, you can claim Ford is bribing taxpayers with their own money, but people like getting money."I think a lot of people are struggling right now, but a onetime payment right before an election isn\'t going to solve the affordability crisis for Ontarians," NDP Leader Marit Stiles said. The leader of the official Opposition said that while few people would say no to getting an extra $200, it won\'t help them pay rent, find a family doctor or deal with tent cities."This is a government that is out of ideas, out of gas and, I think, out of time," Stiles said. Liberal Leader Bonnie Crombie said that she\'ll be donating her cheque to the Ontario Liberal Party to gear up for the next election. In fact, Crombie said these payments are all about the next election."The premier is attempting to bribe Ontarians with their own money. This is taxpayers\' money. What Liberals would do is we would create a middleincome tax cut," Crombie said. So why isn\'t the Ford government doing an acrossthe-board income tax cut like it promised instead of this one-off payment? The answer appears to be twofold, with one part relating to politics and the other to the economy."Tax cuts don\'t sell," one senior Tory said when asked why they aren\'t just cutting taxes.', ' Premier Doug Ford is spending nearly half of a $6.9-billion tax windfall on $200 pre-election "rebate" cheques. Bolstered by higher than projected revenue from personal income tax, corporations tax and sales tax, Ford\'s Progressive Conservatives have earmarked $3 billion to send cheques to 15 million Ontario adults and children in the new year. But Finance Minister Peter Bethlenfalvy\'s fall economic statement tabled Wednesday at Queen\'s Park said the Tories are still running a $6.6-billion deficit. While that\'s lower than the surprise $9.8-billion shortfall for 2024-25 Bethlenfalvy forecast in his March 26 budget, it\'s far from the $200-million surplus he had projected last year. With Ford expected to call a spring election - one year ahead of a scheduled June 2026 vote - Bethlenfalvy hinted to reporters that the books could be balanced as early as his March budget even though he is currently projecting a $1.5-billion deficit for 2025-26."I\'m an optimist, I\'m always hoping I can beat the numbers," he said. In a partisan speech in the legislature, where he twice attacked "the previous Liberal government" in power from 2003 until 2018, Bethlenfalvy painted a rosy picture of Ontario\'s finances."Today we are in a position to do more," the treasurer said, insisting "this government will balance the budget" in 2026-27.Bethlenfalvy defended the Tories\' decision to mail out cheques, first revealed by the Star on Oct. 16, instead of further reducing the deficit to a more manageable $3.6 billion for 2024-25. (He said the government has not calculated the administrative cost of printing and mailing millions of them.)"With our new stronger fiscal position, we can now afford to provide real relief to families to help them in this time of challenge. We know that people aren\'t looking for some money back in time for next year\'s taxes," said the finance minister."They need real support, and they need it now. We are providing $200 per child under the age of 18 - meaning a family of five will receive $1,000," he said."I\'m under no illusions that this will relieve all of the affordability pressures facing Ontario families, but it will help. It\'s real support and, most importantly, it allows the people of Ontario to choose how this money can best help them."Questioning the wisdom of the one-time payments, NDP Leader Marit Stiles said "people in Ontario are tired of gimmicks.""Where are they not spending those dollars right now? Where people really need them," said Stiles, referring to a severe shortage of housing and family doctors and growing homeless encampments."People deserve a government that puts their tax dollars to work and spends (them) responsibly to make life easier. With Doug Ford, you\'re not getting what you paid for," she said. Liberal Leader Bonnie Crombie said Bethlenfalvy\'s mini-budget fails to "address the issues that really matter to Ontario families.""Instead of making real investments to keep emergency rooms open, helping the over 2.5 million people without a family doctor, addressing the urgent need for long-term financial relief, or making housing more affordable, Doug Ford introduced yet another failed fall economic statement that puts Doug Ford\'s rich friends first, and you and your family last," said Crombie."People are dying on wait-lists and Doug Ford is spending billions on booze, foreign spas and the Greenbelt scandal," she said, referring to the expansion of beer and wine sales, the Ontario Place redevelopment and the RCMP investigation into the $8.28-billion Greenbelt land swap debacle. Green Leader Mike Schreiner said there are better ways to spend $3 billion of public money for the greater good of all Ontarians."Two hundred dollars isn\'t going to buy them a home or pay the rent or boost somebody from a tent (encampment) to permanent supportive housing," said Schreiner, who plans to donate his $200 cheque to charity. On the growing problem of homelessness, the organization representing 29 of Ontario\'s largest cities expressed disappointment that there was nothing new to address encampments, addictions and mental health issues."Municipalities have done everything we can, but we don\'t have the resources or expertise to take this on alone," Ontario Big City Mayors said in a statement. Bethlenfalvy bristled at that, noting the province has already raised annual funding for the Homelessness Prevention Program by $200 million. He said that was a 40 per cent hike "in one year upfront (that) continues for the next five years, which is about a $1 billion increase to to help municipalities as we work together on the challenges of homelessness."The fall economic statement came against the backdrop of Ontario\'s debt skyrocketing to a projected $439 billion this year since Ford took office in 2018.That\'s up $116 billion - or 36 per cent - from $323 billion left by the previous Liberal government six years ago. However, interest on the provincial debt is expected to dip by $1.2 billion to $12.7 billion - more than the budget of every department except the Ministry of Health, the Ministry of Education and the Ministry of Children, Community and Social Services. The annual cost of servicing the debt, which is the largest of any subnational jurisdiction in the world, is anticipated to increase to $14.5 billion in two years."Ontario now has the lowest borrowing costs of any province in Canada, saving taxpayers $1.2 billion that we are now able to reinvest back into people," boasted Bethlenfalvy."In fact, our interest on debt relative to revenues is currently at its lowest level since the 1980s and our debt to GDP ratio, which is a measure of our fiscal health, remains at the best level it\'s been in a decade. This is very good news for Ontario taxpayers. It means that when the province needs to borrow, we can do it at a lower cost."The costs of abiding by a court ruling that struck down the Bill 124 salary restraint legislation for public servants, which limited pay hikes to one per cent, has resulted in retroactive raises for workers totalling $6.7 billion.', ' Why is Doug Ford promising to send a $200 payment to every Ontarian? To put it bluntly, because he can. Ford made official what had been reported weeks ago that the fall economic statement will include a tax rebate - "Dougie Dollars" if you will."We\'re able to provide the relief because inflation has increased provincial sales tax revenues and because of the federal government\'s recent changes to their capital gains tax," Ford said. Liberal Leader Bonnie Crombie said that she\'ll be donating her cheque to the Ontario Liberal Party to gear up for the next election. In fact, Crombie said these payments are all about the next election."The premier is attempting to bribe Ontarians with their own money. This is taxpayers\' money. What Liberals would do is we would create a middleincome tax cut," Crombie said. So why isn\'t the Ford government doing an acrossthe-board income tax cut like it promised instead of this one-off payment? The answer appears to be twofold, with one part relating to politics and the other to the economy."Tax cuts don\'t sell," one senior Tory said when asked why they aren\'t just cutting taxes.']

Representative_Docs: [' Colleges in Ontario are in deep financial trouble, leading many of the once-booming institutions to make unprecedented cutbacks to programming and staffing levels in recent months. One of the biggest announcements came last week, when St. Lawrence College in Kingston said it would be cutting 55 programs - a 40-per-cent reduction. Soon after, Loyalist College in Belleville also announced it was cutting 24 programs and laying off 20 per cent of staff. They joined a growing list of Ontario colleges to announce drastic cuts in recent months. Those cuts have come in the form of program suspensions, staffing reductions and closures of physical campus space in the wake of the federal government\'s decision in early 2024 to cap the number of international students allowed in Canada. This policy change has led to a steep decline in international student enrolment at post-secondary institutions throughout the country, and is hitting Ontario colleges particularly hard. Glenn Vollebregt, president and CEO of St. Lawrence College in Kingston, said the change has led to an enrol- ment drop of about 5,000 students, most of them international. Instead of around 12,000 students, they project less than 7,000 will be enrolled by September. This translates to a revenue drop of nearly 70 per cent."That becomes a very difficult operating model for us," Vollebregt said."When you couple that with the fact we are the lowest funded college system in Canada, and we have the lowest tuition in Canada - when you put those two things together, we have a challenge."The steep decline in international student enrolment has led to extraordinary cuts throughout the entire college sector, and it\'s had major ripple effects on their operations as they\'ve come to rely on the tuition fees paid by non-domestic students to help keep them afloat. The Ontario Public Service Employees Union (OPSEU), which represents more than 45,000 college faculty and support staff at the province\'s 24 public colleges, pointed out there\'s been a series of other cuts at its facilities across Ontario. In January, Centennial College announced it would be suspending 49 programs, or 28 per cent of overall programing. College president and CEO Craig Stephenson said the institution was adapting to changes to the federal government\'s immigration policy that led to a drop in international student enrolments, which significantly impacted the college\'s financial standing. Also, Mohawk College will eliminate 127 positions, 20 per cent of its full- and part-time support staff. Sheridan College is suspending 40 programs and laying off staff. Fanshawe College is cutting 18 programs amid a $35-million deficit this year, which it anticipates will grow to a whopping $60 million deficit in 2026 due to the federal government\'s decision. Seneca College\'s Markham site and Algonquin College\'s Perth site are the first campuses to shutter entirely, effective January 2025 and August 2026, respectively. Each of those colleges attributed the cuts to changes to the federal government\'s immigration policy, but the union says it runs deeper than that. OPSEU says since 2010, provincial grants and revenues from private sources have remained relatively stable in other provinces, while provincial funding has shrunk by 28 per cent in Ontario."Not only has (Premier Doug) Ford walked away from post-secondary education, he\'s shifted the responsibility of financing our colleges, a public good, onto students and institutions," JP Hornick, president of OPSEU and faculty at George Brown College, said in a prepared statement."It\'s negligent, and a failed formula sinking the system." HOW MANY COLLEGES ARE IN ONTARIO, AND HOW MANY HAVE ANNOUNCED CUTS?There are 24 public colleges in Ontario. At least eight institutions have publicly announced cuts in some form, including reductions in programming, staffing or physical campus closures. Vollebregt said the issues were plaguing the entire system, and that it\'s been building for years."It wouldn\'t surprise me if you see an nnouncement every couple of weeks from here \'til March," he said. WHAT IS DRIVINGTHE CUTS AT ONTARIO COLLEGES?In January 2024, the federal government announced it would be capping the amount of international students allowed in Canada. At the time, Immigration, Refugees, and Citizenship Canada announced it would reduce the amount of permits for international students by 35 per cent over 2023.It said the policy change was in response to "rapid increases in the number of international students arriving in Canada" which putee on "housing, health pressure care and other services."The decision was cemented thisyear when it announced a further reduction in the intake cap, droppingit another 10 per cent from the 2024 target of 485,000. This year, it plans to issue a total of 437,000 study permits. WHEN DID THE PROBLEMS BEGIN FOR ONTARIO COLLEGES?While the funding challenges were exacerbated by policy changes at the federal level, the problem has been building for years."Colleges have been underfunded for over a decade," Vollebregt said. According to Colleges Ontario, the association which represents public colleges in Ontario, the provincial government provides the smallest per-capita funding of post-secondary education in the country, an issue the college sector has long lobbied the province to correct. It\'s been that way since at least 2012, Vollebregt said, and it was made worse with a tuition freeze in 2019. At that time, the province reduced tuition by 10 per cent, and it has been frozen at that rate ever since. The move was aimed at increasing the affordability of college and university for Ontario students to "help people get the training they need to get good-paying jobs."The government had good intentions, but Vollebregt says it leaves colleges in a tough spot when dealing funding in 2012 dollars, and expenses are in 2025."There\'s a gap there," he said. HOW HAV E COLLEGES DEALT WITH LOWER- THANAVERAGE FUNDINGP To make up for the gap, colleges have relied more heavily on international student tuition. A steep drop in international students means an even steeper drop in revenue. Without the extra revenue generated by international students, Vollebregt said colleges can Ino longer afford to offer certain programming. When deciding which programs to cut in Kingston, Brockville and Cornwall, officials considered three factors, he said. They asked whether the program was financially sustainable, what the projected enrolment would be, and whether it met a labour market need."The reality is, because we have a student population of 12,000 students and the revenue that\'s associated with that, we were able to subsidize those programs that were not financially sustainable on their own," he said."If you take away that income 1OW, with that drop, we had to reduce our program intake for programs that are not financially sustainable on their own."HOW ARE COLLEGES FUNDED?Post-secondary institutions in Ontario receive funding for domestic students through a mix of provincial funding and tuition fees. That funding ratio is complicated, Vollebregt said, but it\'s approximately 60 per cent government funding to 40 per cent tuition. They do not receive funding for international students, leading them to pay higher tuition rates. HOW MUCH TUITION DO INTERNATIONAL STUDENTS PAY?According to Statistics Canada, the number of international students enrolled in Canadian public post-secondary educational institutions more than doubled in a decade, rising from 142,200 in 2010-2011 to 388,800 in 2019-2020.StatsCan also says international undergraduates pay almost five times more on average in tuition fees than Canadian students. The average tuition fees of undergraduate Canadian students rose by 27.8 per cent in 2010-2011 to $6,580 in 2020-2021, while those for undergraduate international students almost doubled to $32,039."Because tuition fees and enrolments of international students are growing at a much faster pace than their Canadian counterparts, their overall contribution to total tuition revenues at Canadian universities has risen. This has helped to make up for the reduction of provincial funding in universities\' budgets for their operational activities," StatsCan said in a 2024 report. WHAT DOES THE SECTOR NEED IN ORDER TO G ET BACK TO NORMAL?OPSEU says an emergency infusion of $1.4 billion is needed to stabilize the college system. Vollebregt agreed that investment into the sector is necessary. He said across the province, colleges are reducing operations and program offerings to become more sustainable, but he argued it\'s counterintuitive since post-secondary education is \'an incredibly valuable investment for any government, when you consider that highly trained and motivated graduates drive industry and help grow the economy."But now, more than ever, the need to fund colleges has reached an all-time high. That\'s what the sector needs so it can get back on its feet, Vollebregt said."Rather than one specifc thing, it\'s really an investment into the college system," he said."We\'re looking for partners to invest into us by the provincial government so that we can deliver on the provincial economic agenda and provide the talent that our economy needs, our local communities need.
