Representative_Docs: [' Progressive Conservative Leader Doug Ford said Friday he is "really, really confident" the much-delayed Eglinton Crosstown LRT will open this year."Well, what I\'m hearing from Metrolinx (is) everything\'s up and going. I guess they are doing training right now on it," Ford said at an election campaign stop in Scarborough."And as soon as everyone is trained, I\'m really, really confident that it will be opening this year."While also touting his plan to build a tunnel under Highway 401, Ford added, "I can\'t give you an exact day or month, but (the Eglinton Crosstown LRT) will be open this year. And we\'re going to train people to make sure it\'s safe. That\'s the number one priority."In a statement Friday, Metrolinx, the provincial agency overseeing the Eglinton LRT, did not directly comment on Ford\'s promise."We continue to make progress on the Eglinton Crosstown LRT, with testing and commissioning still underway," said spokesperson Andrea Ernesaks. "As noted previously, we need to have confidence that key milestones are being met, and once we have a credible schedule, we will share that with the public."Stuart Green, spokesperson to the TTC, who will operate the light rail line once it opens said Friday he didn\'t have any updates on an opening date. "It would be up to Metrolinx (and) the province to announce that," he added."Promised opening dates have come and gone before," said Nigel Morton, a spokesperson for the transit advocacy group TTCriders, said in a statement Friday. "Transit costs have skyrocketed under Metrolinx and the public can\'t get basic answers about why long-overdue LRTs aren\'t open."The multibillion-dollar Eglinton LRT, which has been under construction for 13 years, has run significantly over budget and has missed multiple deadlines for opening. As the Star reported in August 2024, Ford\'s office directed Metrolinx to keep the opening date of the LRT a secret because it had doubts the date would be met. Late last year, TTC chair Jamaal Myers said TTC staff were using June 1, 2025 as a target date to train the LRT drivers. The internal target dates were partly created for financial planning purposes and are not specific to the LRT.Metrolinx CEO Phil Verster - who oversaw construction of both the Eglinton and Finch West LRTs, and promised to give three months\' notice on the Eglinton LRT\'s opening date - announced his departure from the provincial transit agency in December. Earlier that same month, Verster said he expected the Eglinton LRT to be completed "in the new year" after contractors recently identified a software design flaw in the line\'s signalling system. After appointing Infrastructure Ontario CEO Michael Lindsay as the interim Metrolinx head in December, Ford said he had given "a clear mandate to open Eglinton Crosstown as soon as it is safe to do so."', ' Phil Verster, the embattled head of Metrolinx, is leaving the transit agency. As first reported by the Star on Monday, Verster will soon depart the organization he has led for more than seven years. Sources close to him, speaking confidentially to discuss Verster\'s departure, confide that he is headed overseas to run a major rail system. His last day at Metrolinx is Dec. 16.Premier Doug Ford said Infrastructure Ontario president and CEO Michael Lindsay would serve as interim Metrolinx boss starting next Monday."I have given Michael a clear mandate to open Eglinton Crosstown as soon as it is safe to do so. That is his top priority," said Ford, who was informed by Verster last Friday that he was resigning for a new post. Verster has faced criticism for the continued delays in completing the Crosstown line that has been under construction for 13 years."I want to thank Phil for his many years of service to Ontario. Phil led and supported explosive growth in transit construction, including the largest expansion of public transit in North America," the premier said."The transportation landscape in Ontario will be permanently better because of his contributions," Ford said, noting the province is spending some $70 billion over the next decade on public transit expansion. A high-profile executive who ran transit systems in England, Scotland and Ireland before coming to Ontario, Verster made $838,097 last year as president and CEO of Metrolinx. Ford predicted the transit boss would be earning even more in his new job abroad."He\'s had offers for years for three times as much to run a railroad. We got a deal with Phil Verster," the premier told Globe and Mail reporter Laura Stone. Metrolinx\'s board of directors will soon begin seeking a permanent replacement for Verster. While he was an appointee of Liberal premier Kathleen Wynne, he became a favourite of Ford, who frequently defended him over delays to the still incomplete Eglinton Crosstown. Indeed, the premier praised Verster as "an all-star" and a "champion" even as there was frustration about the Eglinton Crosstown, which broke ground in 2011.The opposition New Democrats had repeatedly called upon the Tories to sack the transit boss."Why has this government let Metrolinx\'s Phil Vester continue to drive this train, overrun and overbudget and over-delayed?" NDP MPP Jill Andrew (St. Paul\'s) told the house about an hour before the Star revealed Verster\'s departure. Green MPP Aislinn Clancy (Kitchener Centre) said "under Phil Verster\'s tenure, Metrolinx has made mistake after mistake and cost our province billions."Mr. Verster\'s departure is an important first step toward delivering the accountability that the people of this province deserve."But let\'s remember that the buck ultimately stops with the premier, who has been propping up Metrolinx\'s failures for six years now," said Clancy. Verster was not available for comment Monday, and neither was Transportation Minister Prabmeet Sarkaria. Metrolinx did not respond to media queries. At city hall, Coun. Mike Colle (Ward 8, Eglinton-Lawrence) was blunt."Hallelujah! Good riddance. He\'s put us through hell. Total incompetence. Total mismanagement. Total burning of money," said Colle."He\'s the worst thing that has happened to this city since Hurricane Hazel," said the councillor, whose ward includes the Eglinton Crosstown."He basically took over a multibillion-dollar transit project that we all had high hopes for to relieve the congestion in the city. And all he\'s done is spend billions with no results, no success."Mayor Olivia Chow was more measured, thanking Verster for "seven years of dedication to public transit and serving the people of Ontario.""The priority for the next CEO must be getting transit projects completed and open because we share the same goal - getting Toronto moving," said Chow. Verster\'s defenders insist any delays are due to his cautious nature, which is one reason why he has consistently pledged to give three months\' notice to the public before the line opens, which sparked consternation at Queen\'s Park. Last week, Verster told a Metrolinx board meeting he expects the Eglinton Crosstown to be finished and ready to carry passengers "in the new year."He said contractors recently identified a software design flaw in the line\'s signalling system, posing a safety risk "that\'s unacceptable for operations."That repair will be done by the end of this month."There\'s no compromise on safety or on the quality of our operations," he told the board, explaining the testing is about 95 to 96 per cent complete. Verster also said the Finch West LRT has made "significant progress" with major construction done on all its stations. But its opening date also remains up in the air. With files from Mahdis Habibinia', ' There is nothing like an election campaign to make politicians suddenly find money to spend, so it\'s not surprising that provincial party leaders came to town last week to dole out megabucks for transit. City politicians are, of course, happy to take the hypothetical money, but they may be forfeiting our right to build and run our own transit system. PC Leader Doug Ford and Liberal Leader Bonnie Crombie both promised to "upload" to the province the cost of Ottawa\'s beleaguered LRT, which could run into billions of dollars. Ford would give responsibility for the LRT to Metrolinx, the provincial transportation agency that now runs GO Transit in the Greater Toronto Area. Crombie would not, doubting Metrolinx\'s ability to do the job, but it\'s unclear how she would go about it. Mayor Mark Sutcliffe, who has lobbied hard for more transit money, and transit commission chair Glen Gower pulled out the superlatives. A "game-changer," Sutcliffe called Ford\'s promise, while Gower likened it to a "moon landing" for city council. But remember that the funding announcement is just a campaign promise - and you decide how much of a pre - mium to put on such promises by politicians in an election. Potentially however, Ottawa could save billions of dollars and eliminate the constant pressure on its budget if the province were to take over LRT and build Stage 3 to Barrhaven and Kanata. "Their No. 1 anchor around their neck is the cost of this LRT," said Ford, who put what the city would save at about $4 billion over 30 years. "We are going to take the burden off Ottawa." If Ford wins and keeps his promise, what kind of transit system would we have in Ottawa? In the euphoria of the moment, no one is asking this key question. But it needs asking. Uploading something means the entity assuming responsibility takes over the service in question. They pay for it and they run it. Let\'s not forget that Metrolinx has been under fire for the ballooning cost of a 19-km Eglinton Crosstown light transit system that is in its 14th year of construction. The cost ballooned from $9.1 billion in 2011 to $12.8 billion today. The line was supposed to be completed in 2020, but is now set to open this year. Metrolinx has also been criticized for lack of transparency. And this is the body that will take over Ottawa LRT under Ford\'s plan. This means decisions on our transit would likely be made in Toronto by people who don\'t live in the city, perhaps don\'t really know it and, crucially, are not answerable to Ottawa taxpayers or riders. This is why the Liberals say they won\'t hand over Ottawa transit to Metrolinx, saying such a move would be a "recipe for a disaster."There are important questions about Metrolinx taking over LRT, if the plan does come to pass. By virtue of building and owning the LRT, Metrolinx will run the service. Which raises questions about OC Transpo\'s future role. Might it become redundant? The city\'s bus and rail systems are integrated, so it\'s difficult to see how Metrolinx will run LRT and not the buses. Come to think of it, what happens to the oversight of the transit commission? Will council have any say or responsibility for the city\'s transit? If there are problems with the service, who do riders complain to? OC Transpo or Metrolinx in downtown Toronto? No one really knows. The devil, of course, is in the details. All Sutcliffe will say is that there will be hard negotiations over the fine print."We need to see what it\'s going to mean and how we will be able to put this arrangement together," he said. For now, the city is all about the promise of getting billions from the province. We may yet get the money, but there is no telling whether we\'ll get a transit system Ottawans want and need, or just one made in Toronto. Mohammed Adam is an Ottawa journalist and commentator. Reach him at nylamiles48@gmail. com']

Representative_Docs: [' Premier Doug Ford is downplaying NDP accusations that internal emails reveal inconsistencies in government Greenbelt testimony to Ontario\'s ethics watchdog."I don\'t know anything about it," Ford told the Star at the new Bombardier business jet factory at Pearson International Airport on Monday. Through a freedom of information request, the New Democrats obtained an email exchange the opposition party charged contradicts statements given under oath to the integrity commissioner last year. As first reported by the Star, the issue revolves around an Oct. 17, 2022 email - on private accounts instead of government servers - between Patrick Sackville, then Ford\'s principal secretary and now his chief of staff, and Ryan Amato, at the time the top aide to then-municipal affairs minister Steve Clark. The auditor noted "forwarding government information to personal accounts is not appropriate because of cybersecurity concerns" and that "using nongovernment resources to conduct government business is unacceptable."In response, the Tories are tackling all 15 of the recommendations made in the report that probed the removal of 7,400 acres from the two-million-acre environmentally sensitive Greenbelt around the Greater Toronto and Hamilton Area to build housing. The most significant of those recommendations - cancelling the land swap - was addressed by Ford on Sept. 21 after a separate Greenbelt report on Aug. 30 by the integrity commissioner. In their parallel probes, the auditor general and integrity commissioner found certain developers with Tory connections were "favoured" in a process supposedly led by Amato, who was Clark\'s chief of staff. Amato, who has maintained he "acted appropriately," resigned on Aug. 22, while Clark, who remains the MPP for Leeds-Grenville-Thousand Islands and Rideau Lakes, quit Ford\'s cabinet on Sept. 4.The premier has insisted he was not aware of how the 15 parcels of land were selected for removal from the Greenbelt, a rezoning change estimated to be worth $8.28 billion to landowners."I had nothing to do with the changes in the Greenbelt ... the auditor general cleared us, cleared my office, and the integrity commissioner cleared me and my office," Ford said Oct. 31.But when he scrapped the land swap, which is now being investigated by the RCMP, he acknowledged "it was a mistake to open the Greenbelt.""I made a promise to you that I wouldn\'t touch the Greenbelt. I broke that promise," the premier said last September. The scandal also led Ford to part ways with Kaleed Rasheed, who was turfed as public and business service delivery minister and from the PC caucus, and Jae Truesdell, who was the premier\'s housing adviser. That\'s because Rasheed and Truesdell were on a controversial 2020 trip to Las Vegas with Greenbelt developer Shakir Rehmatullah and Amin Massoudi, Ford\'s then principal secretary.', ' A recently discovered internal email related to the $8.28-billion Greenbelt scandal suggests Doug Ford\'s office "was far more involved" in the controversial land swap than the premier has maintained. In a message from Amato to Sackville that day, the ministerial chief of staff shared a "list of criteria for removals" of 7,400 acres from the two-million-acre environmentally sensitive Greenbelt around the Greater Toronto and Hamilton Area. These included "infrastructure services," such as nearby roads, gas and water mains, hydro lines, police and fire services, among other things. It also listed "potential offsets" such as the Paris Galt Moraine "green space our government has decided not to move on" and "options to go larger depending on executive interest."The timing of the email is at odds with testimony made under oath to J. David Wake, the integrity commissioner, for his Aug. 31 report on the Greenbelt land swap."Members of the premier\'s staff also told us they were not involved in the selection of properties," wrote Wake."Mr. Sackville said he did not discuss specific properties to be removed or removal criteria with Mr. Amato until the briefing that occurred on October 27, 2022," the ethics watchdog continued."Mr. Sackville recalled being first briefed about the Greenbelt project at a meeting facilitated by the cabinet office on October 27, 2022. He told me that he recalled the intentions of the policy were discussed and that it should be \'programmatic,\' meaning that it should be something that could be repeated and made standard."But that was 10 days after the Oct. 17 email in which criteria for removal of the lands from the Greenbelt were addressed. Clark announced the changes on Nov. 4, 2022."This email ... shows that the premier\'s office was far more involved than Mr. Ford claims in the selection of Greenbelt lands for removal," said NDP Leader Marit Stiles."Conservatives very much want their Greenbelt scandal to go away, but it is glaringly clear they can\'t hide from what they\'ve done," said Stiles, who has asked Wake to "provide an opinion on whether it is consistent with Mr. Sackville\'s testimony to your office under oath.""With each new piece of evidence, we are seeing more cracks in the narrative Mr. Ford and his insiders have been trying desperately to get people to believe - that Ford was in the dark about this scheme to carve up prime farmland and green space for land speculators," she said. I will get back to you as soon as I have had an opportunity to review the matter," Wake wrote her on Jan. 15.Sackville declined to comment when contacted by the Star. But the email was shared with the NDP by cabinet office lawyers as soon as the now chief of staff, who receives hundreds of messages daily, found and forwarded it."This record was just discovered upon deeper review," Sackville wrote on Dec. 20 to cabinet office general counsel Don Fawcett. Two days later, it was handed over to the New Democrats, who had filed a freedom of information request months earlier."To ensure all necessary due diligence was exercised, Patrick Sackville ... conducted additional searches within his personal email account," wrote Janet Dadufalza, senior freedom of information manager in cabinet office."From this search, an email that is considered to be responsive to your request was found. Partial access is granted," she wrote the NDP on Dec. 22.But "access to the remaining record continues to be denied" because of cabinet privilege. It is unclear why personal email accounts were being used to conduct official government business. Amato resigned on Aug. 22. Clark, who remains the MPP for Leeds-Grenville-Thousand Islands and Rideau Lakes, quit Ford\'s cabinet on Sept. 4.Through his lawyer, Kathryn Marshall, Amato declined to comment. I\'m very, very sorry," the premier said that day."I made a promise to you that I wouldn\'t touch the Greenbelt. I broke that promise. As a first step to earning back your trust, I\'ll be reversing the changes. We moved too quickly and we made the wrong decision ... it caused people to question our motives."Other casualties of the imbroglio were Kaleed Rasheed, who was forced out as Ford\'s business minister and turfed from the Progressive Conservative caucus last September, and Jae Truesdell, who was Ford\'s housing adviser. Representative_Docs: [' The LCBO will resume giving paper bags to customers after the ban was sacked by Premier Doug Ford. In an unusual intervention with the operations of the Crown-owned Liquor Control Board of Ontario, Ford ordered the booze giant to rethink its bag policy that took effect last September."I\'m requesting that you take immediate steps to reverse the decision to remove paper bags from the LCBO\'s retail locations," the premier wrote Sunday in a terse letter to George Soleas, president and CEO of the company."At a time when many Ontario families are already struggling to make ends meet, every additional expense counts. That includes charging customers for reusable bags instead of the free paper bags that the LCBO previously offered," wrote Ford."This change has left people stuck openly carrying alcohol in public when leaving a LCBO store," added the premier, a teetotaler. The LCBO, which first announced the phasing out of the paper bags last spring, confirmed Monday it "has received direction from the provincial government to take steps to reintroduce single-use paper bags" at its more than 680 outlets."While we are not able to confirm an availability date at this time, we will share more details with our valued customers in the coming weeks," the company said. Last April 27, Soleas said the scheme would remove about 135 million paper bags from circulation, diverting 2,665 tonnes of waste from landfill. The company maintained at the time that it would save the equivalent of more than 188,000 trees annually. It followed the decision to stop providing customers plastic bags in 2008.But Ford said Sunday that "the environmental merits of this decision are questionable at best.""Paper bags are an easily recyclable alternative to single-use plastic, which is why the LCBO adopted them in the first place," he reminded Soleas."As a government, we are focused on making life easier, more convenient, and more affordable for the people of Ontario. The decision to remove paper bags has had the opposite effect."', ' Bring back the paper bags! That\'s the message from Ontario Premier Doug Ford to the LCBO. Ford has written to LCBO president and CEO George Soleas, telling him to reverse course on his bag policy. The LCBO announced they were phasing out paper bags last August, instead only offering customers the chance to buy recyclable bags or bring their own."This initiative will help to minimize our impact on the environment and create a more sustainable Ontario," the government agency said in a statement. Environmental concerns or not, Ford wants the policy reversed."I\'m requesting that you take immediate steps to reverse the decision to remove paper bags from the LCBO\'s retail locations," Ford wrote."At a time when many Ontario families are already struggling to make ends meet, every additional expense counts. That includes charging customers for reusable bags instead of the free paper bags that the LCBO previously offered."Those reusable bags the LCBO sells go for $1.25 for a bag to carry two bottles, or $2.95 for one to carry six. They also sell a four-pocket organic cotton bag for $14.95, which is not overly affordable, nor is it environmentally friendly. For Ford, his call for the LCBO to bring back paper bags is mostly about affordability."People rightly expect their government - and, by extension, Crown corporations such as the LCBO - to be mindful of these costs and refrain from imposing additional and unnecessary burdens on them," Ford said. He\'s right. I just wish it hadn\'t taken him seven months to tell the LCBO they were on the wrong track. The bags the LCBO now sells are made from recycled plastic water bottles, but unlike the old paper bags aren\'t recyclable themselves - a point Ford makes in his letter."Moreover, the environmental merits of this decision are questionable at best. Paper bags are an easily recyclable alternative to single-use plastic, which is why the LCBO adopted them in the first place," Ford wrote. A study by Denmark\'s Ministry of the Environment and Food found the kind of plastic bags the LCBO is selling would have to be reused eight times to be better than a plastic shopping bag when it comes to climate change. However, the LCBO\'s plastic bags would need to be used 84 times to be better on all environmental indicators. That organic cotton bag they are selling would need to be used a whopping 20,000 times to be better than plastic when all environmental factors are considered. Except, that\'s comparing the reusable bags to plastic bags. The LCBO was previously using paper - an easily recycled product. It\'s been well-documented that we now have a glut of reusable plastic bags in the world, leading many to question whether this is helping or hurting. We all want a cleaner environment. I don\'t know a single person who wants to be polluting, but we aren\'t always smart about policy. This LCBO policy was an attempt by the government agency to look like a good corporate steward, a leader in environmental and sustainability goals. It hasn\'t worked out that way and it has definitely inconvenienced consumers."As a government, we are focused on making life easier, more convenient and more affordable for the people of Ontario. The decision to remove paper bags has had the opposite effect," Ford wrote to Soleas. What will be interesting to find out is how much money the LCBO has been making off the plastic bags they have been selling. The paper bags were obviously a cost to them, but the plastic ones are a potential profit centre. I\'ll still take my reusable bag with me when I plan a trip, but I\'ll also welcome the return of the paper bags for those times when I pop into the LCBO unexpectedly. This is a common-sense move, and a welcome one.', ' Bring back the paper bags! That\'s the message from Ontario Premier Doug Ford to the LCBO. The bags the LCBO now sells are made from recycled plastic water bottles, but unlike the old paper bags aren\'t recyclable themselves - a point Ford makes in his letter."Moreover, the environmental merits of this decision are questionable at best. Paper bags are an easily recyclable alternative to single-use plastic, which is why the LCBO adopted them in the first place," Ford wrote. A study by Denmark\'s Ministry of the Environment and Food found the kind of plastic bags the LCBO is selling would have to be reused eight times to be better than a plastic shopping bag when it comes to climate change. However, the LCBO\'s plastic bags would need to be used 84 times to be better on all environmental indicators. That organic cotton bag they are selling would need to be used a whopping 20,000 times to be better than plastic when all environmental factors are considered. Except, that\'s comparing the reusable bags to plastic bags. The LCBO was previously using paper - an easily recycled product. It\'s been well-documented that we now have a glut of reusable plastic bags in the world, leading many to question whether this is helping or hurting. We all want a cleaner environment. I don\'t know a single person who wants to be polluting, but we aren\'t always smart about policy. This LCBO policy was an attempt by the government agency to look like a good corporate steward, a leader in environmental and sustainability goals. It hasn\'t worked out that way and it has definitely inconvenienced consumers."As a government, we are focused on making life easier, more convenient and more affordable for the people of Ontario. The decision to remove paper bags has had the opposite effect," Ford wrote to Soleas. What will be interesting to find out is how much money the LCBO has been making off the plastic bags they have been selling. The paper bags were obviously a cost to them, but the plastic ones are a potential profit centre. I\'ll still take my reusable bag with me when I plan a trip, but I\'ll also welcome the return of the paper bags for those times when I pop into the LCBO unexpectedly. This is a common-sense move, and a welcome one. blilley@postmedia.com @brianlilley']

Representative_Docs: [' In a victory for nurses, teachers and thousands of unionized public sector workers, Ontario\'s top court has upheld a ruling that Premier Doug Ford\'s wage restraint legislation is unconstitutional. The Court of Appeal released a long-awaited decision Monday finding the Progressive Conservative government infringed upon Charter rights to collective bargaining with Bill 124.The legislation capped wage increases for most public sector workers at one per cent annually for three years and has been blamed for an exodus of health-care workers during the COVID-19 pandemic as they toiled long hours at the risk of their own health."Ontario has failed to demonstrate that the Act is minimally impairing of the respondents\' collective bargain rights," said the court\'s decision. Unifor President Lana Payne hailed the decision, calling it "a victory for free and fair collective bargaining."Even as public sector unions awaited the ruling, labour arbitrators have been awarding some public sector workers retroactive pay in what has been a period of high inflation because their contracts included "reopener" clauses. The latest such award was an extra 6.5 per cent for members of the Ontario Public Service Employees Union. Nurses, some teachers and hospital workers including cooks, lab technicians, personal support workers and dietary aides have also been awarded pay increases. The sudden shift came Monday evening after Ontario\'s top court upheld a Superior Court ruling that Bill 124 was unconstitutional and union leaders signalled they were out of patience. A terse statement from the office of Attorney General Doug Downey said the government "will not appeal today\'s Court of Appeal decision and will instead take steps to repeal Bill 124 in its entirety in the coming weeks."The statement was unexpected. Just three hours before it was issued, Finance Minister Peter Bethlenfalvy had told a news conference the government would "take ... time" to consider whether to seek leave to appeal the ruling to the Supreme Court of Canada."Every climbdown and policy reversal is proof that when we work together, we can win," NDP Leader Marit Stiles - whose party had long called for the repeal of the 2019 legislation - said on social media."After wasting years and countless dollars fighting workers in court, it\'s time to start fixing the mess Bill 124 created in our hospitals, schools and public services," Stiles said. In its long-awaited decision Monday morning, the Court of Appeal found the Progressive Conservative government infringed upon Charter rights to collective bargaining with Bill 124.The legislation capped wage increases for most public-sector workers at one per cent annually for three years and has been blamed for an exodus of health-care workers during the COVID-19 pandemic as they toiled long hours at the risk of their own health."Ontario has not been able to explain why wage restraint could not have been achieved through good-faith bargaining," judges Lise Favreau and David Doherty wrote in their majority decision. In a dissenting opinion, a third judge on the appeal panel, William Hourigan, said courts are "public policy amateurs.""Thus, it is not the role of judges to second-guess the policy choice made by governments," Hourigan said. The government\'s reversal follows its decision in September to drop plans to open more of the ecologically sensitive Greenbelt in the Greater Toronto and Hamilton Area to development. The Royal Canadian Mounted Police are investigating "irregularities" in the government\'s original plan, including whether developers were tipped off in advance. The attorney general\'s statement hinted at other measures coming soon to help those impacted by the wage restraint legislation."To solve for the inequality of workers created by today\'s court decision, the province will urgently introduce regulations to exempt non-unionized and non-associated workers from Bill 124 until it is repealed."The challenge to Bill 124 was brought by teachers unions, the Ontario Nurses\' Association, the Ontario Public Service Employees Union, Unifor and the Power Workers\' Union, among others representing 2,500 bargaining units. Among other things, they argued Bill 124 was unfair because it exempted police and firefighters - both male-dominated occupations - from the wage caps."Let the court\'s ruling be a lesson for the Ford government to never circumvent bargaining or trample on worker democratic rights again," said Karen Brown, president of the Elementary Teachers\' Federation of Ontario."This government does not respect workers," said René Jansen in de Wal, president of the Ontario English Catholic Teachers\' Association, calling the province\'s appeal of the initial ruling "reckless" and "a waste of tax dollars."Bethlenfalvy acknowledged the legislation "continues to impact a lot of people" and said he did not have a tally of the government\'s legal costs. Liberal labour critic John Fraser, MPP for Ottawa South, estimated the amount in the "millions of dollars.""Nothing to show for it," he added. Ontario Nurses\' Association president Erin Ariss, other union leaders and opposition parties at Queen\'s Park before Bethlenfalvy spoke had urged the province not to attempt an appeal."Since Doug Ford took office in 2018, the number of nurses leaving the system has increased every year. For every 10 nurses this government says have been hired, six have left," Ariss said. Ontario Liberal Leader Bonnie Crombie congratulated the unions on a "long-overdue victory ... for the workers who play such important roles in our lives."Even as public-sector unions awaited the ruling, labour arbitrators have been awarding some public-sector workers retroactive pay in what has been a period of high inflation because their contracts included "reopener" clauses. The latest such award was an extra 6.5 per cent for members of the Ontario Public Service Employees Union. Nurses, some teachers and hospital workers, including cooks, lab technicians, personal support workers and dietary aides, have also been awarded pay increases. But thousands of public-sector workers without "reopener" clauses have no such remedy - something the unions said they intend to address through pressure on the government, although the process is unclear."We want to ensure everyone gets something," said Ontario Federation of Labour president Laura Walton, noting unionized workers should not have to wait until their contracts are up for renegotiation. "No worker should be left behind."Bethlenfalvy said the cost of reopeners and catch-ups has been "incorporated" into the government\'s spending plans but did not provide a dollar figure, calling it a "moving" target. High inflation in the last couple of years has worsened the impact of Bill 124 on workers, putting them further behind in terms of purchasing power and in need of a catch-up, union leaders said. A previous Liberal government\'s Bill 115, which imposed wages on teachers and education workers, was struck down as unconstitutional a decade ago. As part of the remedy process, a judge instructed the government and unions to reach an agreement. The government subsequently awarded more than $200 million to the impacted workers. Ontario\'s independent Financial Accountability Office warned 18 months ago it may cost the province $8.4 billion in suppressed wages if Bill 124 was struck down. The estimate was based on the one per cent cap in the legislation and historical trends in provincial public-sector wage increases. Monday\'s ruling followed the government\'s appeal of a 2022 decision by the Ontario Superior Court of Justice that the wage restraint legislation - passed as an austerity measure to help balance the budget before the COVID-19 pandemic emerged - violated Charter rights to collective bargaining."On my view of the evidence, Ontario was not facing a situation in 2019 that justified an infringement on Charter rights," Justice Markus Koehnen wrote in his original ruling. "Unlike other cases that have upheld wage restraint legislation, Bill 124 sets the wage cap at a rate below which employees were obtaining in free collective bargaining negotiations."']

Name: 21_land_development_urban_appeal
Representative_Docs: [' A provincial law change that curtailed third-party groups\' ability to appeal development decisions has left environmental and ratepayer groups saying they\'ve been silenced in a move that puts developer interests ahead of citizen concerns. Ontario residents can no longer appeal development decisions at the Ontario Land Tribunal - a quasi-judicial body designed to adjudicate planning and other land disputes - after the Doug Ford government introduced legislation that removes the ability of third-parties such as ratepayer groups or environmental groups to do so. The province says the changes to the third-party appeal rights in the Cutting Red Tape to Build More Homes Act (Bill 185), which passed in June, will "help communities get quicker planning approvals for housing projects."But critics say the legislation is another attack on "citizen rights" and the public\'s participation in the development process and will ultimately lead to poorly planned and less safe communities across the province."This is the loss of an important mechanism for the public to make sure that environmental and public health concerns were raised and properly considered in development decisions across the province," said Jacqueline Wilson, counsel for the Canadian Environmental Law Association, who says his organization has been part of local resident appeals for decades."It\'s really a problem to cut out active engaged citizens, who deeply care about their communities, from the equation."According to the OLT, between April 1, 2022, to March 31, 2023, the Tribunal handled 1,422 cases, totalling 2,161 appeals. The OLT said they don\'t track the number of appeals made by developers versus individuals or third-party groups. However, since the law came into effect in June, 62 third-party appeals that didn\'t "meet the transition provisions," which include a hearing date scheduled before April 10, 2024, were dismissed, a spokesperson for the OLT said. The new legislation places restrictions on the ability of the public to appeal amendments to official plans and zoning bylaws made through development applications. The only groups who can appeal are "public bodies," specified persons who are defined as government, utility boards, and agencies. Landowners and developers can also appeal municipal development decisions they don\'t agree with. Justine Teplycky, a spokesperson for Housing Minister Paul Calandra, says the changes to the legislation "provide the appropriate balance between speeding up planning approvals and maintaining an avenue for impacted landowners to voice their concerns."She says between 2021 and 2023, approximately 67,000 housing units were subject to third-party appeals of official plans and rezoning. Teplycky says "the public still has opportunities to provide full input in the planning process to their locally elected councils, who are best positioned to make decisions that reflect the needs of their communities."Environmental lawyer David Donnelly says in his research of third-party appeals, he believes just a handful of appeals in the GTA have hindered or slowed down the process. Some residents whose cases have been dismissed this past month also disagree with the notion their voices are better heard at the municipal level. Suzi Recine, with the group Friends to Conserve Kleinburg, who had filed an appeal at the OLT against plans to build about 800 single-detached homes and townhomes on part of the Copper Creek golf club in Vaughan, said the community turned to the OLT once they realized they had no support from the city and there was a "lack of consideration of their concerns.""This was a way for residents to have a voice. Why are we being silenced?" said Recine. "Bills like Bill 185 ... give more powers to the government and developers, while taking away the public\'s opportunity to be heard."The Copper Creek community is owned by both Fieldgate Developments and by TACC Developments, development companies run by Jack Eisenberger and Silvio De Gasperis. The development is being built by Block 55 Northwest Landowners Group Inc., which consists of three landowners, said Alana De Gasperis, a spokesperson for TACC Developments. Recine says the residents appealed the development to the OLT amidst concerns of overdevelopment of the pristine area, and environmental degradation of an area that borders the Greenbelt and the Humber River watershed. In a statement, Alana De Gasperis said there have been "numerous opportunities for public input" in addition to statutory public hearings. She also said the TACC and the landowners have worked with staff to preserve trees, create a buffer zone between the new and existing communities, and ensure appropriate environmental protections are in place, including the completion of several studies that have been reviewed by the city and the conservation authority. She said the appeal, which was previously dismissed by the OLT and heard at Divisional Court, has "delayed the project approximately 3 years."Recine says her group\'s case was dismissed by the OLT in July, despite having been given a hearing date prior to the bill\'s passing. The Kleinburg group was told on April 10 that their case would be heard in June 2025.Recine said within hours of their hearing being scheduled, the province introduced Bill 185, which included transition provisions that said any third-party appeal that didn\'t have a hearing date scheduled prior to April 10, 2024, was immediately dismissed. And even though the law didn\'t pass until June, this provision was applied retroactively."We got our date, and then a short while later, we found out our entire case was dismissed," said Recine. "Where is the fairness to the residents and the community?"In an email, the province said the law was retroactively applied as that was the day the legislation was introduced, said Teplycky. Environmental lawyer Donnelly said several groups he is representing have had their cases dismissed as a result of Bill 185."It\'s not just about the rights of one group of residents, it\'s about the rights of the public to fight for environmental protections for all," he said. "You should care about the fact that developers have all these rights, and citizens have none."Julie Neves, the chair of Stop Petersburg Sand Pit Inc., says her group\'s appeal of an aggregate pit in Wilmot, Ont., was dismissed in July as her group was not one of the parties allowed to file an appeal per the new legislation. The group had been opposing an application for an aggregate pit, and had tried to petition their town council to monitor the air quality in the area where six others already operate, to find ways to "clean them up and improve conditions."When those efforts failed, Neves\' group filed an appeal with the OLT. But that appeal route was dismissed before it even began, she said."At this point, all our citizen rights have been taken away," said Neves. "There are no more options left ... and the development always gets its way."Justin Sherwood, a spokesperson with the Building Industry and Land Development Association (BILD), said they support "efforts to increase the speed and efficiency of the approvals process" but says it\'s too early to know if this move by the province will do just that."We understand, and can appreciate, that one of the intentions to limit third party appeals was to eliminate those that were frivolous or vexatious. However, the results and outcome of this are yet to be tested since the legislation was only passed in early June," said Sherwood. The OLT is the latest iteration of what has been more commonly known as the Ontario Municipal Board and the Local Planning Appeal Tribunal - administrative tribunals that were created to adjudicate planning matters. The OLT was created in 2021, after the government consolidated several different boards including the Conservation Review Board, the Environmental Review Tribunal, the Local Planning Appeal Tribunal and the Mining and Lands Tribunal. Donnelly said removing third party appeals - or what he calls "citizen appeals" - at the OLT has little to do with NIMBYs (not-in-my-backyard), a term that refers to those who oppose development in their own neighbourhoods. He fears it will instead remove the ability of concerned citizens and environmental groups who have historically used the OLT (and its predecessors) to push cities and developers to make better planning decisions."Nobody has made the case that having residents, neighbours, environmentalists, First Nations involved in the planning process is a bad thing. They have always been the check and the balance in the system, and now that\'s being taken away," Donnelly said. He cites several cases where appeals led to outcomes in the public interest, including the enactment of the Oak Ridges Moraine Protection Act, which came as the result of a 12-month appeal by a third-party group called Save the Rouge Valley System Inc. to a development on the environmentally sensitive lands. He said other appeals against aggregate quarries and mines have led the projects to be denied, or have a significantly reduced footprint. CELA lawyer Wilson says that without a place for the public to appeal development decisions, many will have no choice but to turn to the courts by seeking a judicial review of a planning decision, leading to delays and high costs for all parties. Recine says the Kleinburg group has already spent thousands on legal fees and experts at the OLT. In light of the recent dismissal, she says she\'s not sure if the group will continue their fight."I don\'t know where this leaves us," she said. "With a dismissal of the entire case, it leaves us without a voice."', ' A provincial law change that curtailed third-party groups\' ability to appeal development decisions has left environmental and ratepayer groups saying they\'ve been silenced in a move that puts developer interests ahead of citizen concerns. "With a dismissal of the entire case, it leaves us without a voice."', ' Anti-sprawl advocates are warning that newly proposed housing legislation could dislodge Hamilton\'s firm urban boundary if the province follows though. If passed, Bill 185 would allow developers to appeal to the Ontario Land Tribunal (OLT) if municipalities reject applications to expand urban areas or don\'t deal with them within 120 days - new provisions currently unavailable to them."Sprawl developers would be able to force municipalities to consider their demands to extend settlement boundaries at any time and appeal refusals," Phil Pothen, a lawyer and planning expert with advocacy group Environmental Defence, told The Spectator. That\'s a "bid to take away by stealth the victory that Hamilton residents" scored in securing a firm urban boundary, Pothen said. That appeal provision in Bill 185, in combination with new proposed policies governing settlement-area expansions in the province\'s newly drafted provincial policy statement, means developers could challenge council rejections of urban boundary adjustments of any size, noted Steve Robichaud, the city\'s acting general manager of planning and economic development. The proposed provincial policy statement would eliminate a roughly 100-acre cap for privately initiated urban expansions stipulated in the Growth Plan for the Greater Golden Horseshoe, Robichaud explained. Even if approved through the OLT, servicing may not be ready to accommodate homes in would-be urban expansion lands, he said."For some of these areas, even if they were brought into the urban area, the infrastructure may not be readily available to accommodate them."Back-to-back city councils, in response to anti-sprawl advocacy, opted to freeze the urban boundary and direct development to the existing settlement area as part of its long-term growth plan. But that decision spurred pushback from residential developers who had hoped to build houses on parcels of rural land, and criticism from Tory government officials who urged expansion to meet housing goals. The debate boiled over in late 2022, when then-housing minister Steve Clark imposed a roughly 5,000-acre urban expansion on Hamilton that included tracts of farmland in Elfrida and Glanbrook. Then, a year later, new minister Paul Calandra reversed that expansion, along with a slew of other land-use changes the province had forced on municipalities, following a pair of scathing watchdog reports that suggested undue developer and political influence in the government\'s exercise to open up the Greenbelt for housing. Council promptly endorsed the provincial U-turn, despite protests from developers whose plans were suddenly upended."Your response to growth must, respectfully, be realistic. I have seen no evidence that your response to growth is realistic," Nancy Smith, a lawyer representing land owners in Elfrida, the largest of Hamilton\'s would-be expansion areas, told city politicians in November. City politicians who opposed Premier Doug Ford\'s now-abandoned wholesale expansion have asserted Hamilton can meet provincial housing targets by focusing development within the existing urban area by increasing density. Last week, Calandra outlined how Bill 185, the proposed Cutting Red Tape to Build More Homes Act, aims to do away with the current restriction on OLT appeals of rejected urban expansions in concert with a variety of changes meant to advance the government\'s goal of 1.5 million homes by 2031."It\'s how it was done in the Province of Ontario for a number of years and I think it\'s properly done again with an independent third-party adjudicator," he told reporters at Queen\'s Park. In Hamilton, development consortiums still hoping to build on walked-back expansion lands have persisted with appeals to the OLT, but those challenges are more narrowly focused on disputes with the city over site plans, rather than the crucial overarching question of whether land is urban or rural. That includes the Upper West Side group\'s proposal for 5,400 to 7,000 homes on more than 200 acres of land bounded by Upper James Street, Twenty, Dickenson and Glancaster roads near the airport. The appeal wasn\'t launched "in relation to the land uses being proposed, but the manner in which the city has chosen to process applications and technical studies before them," a representative of planning consultant Corbett Land Strategies Ltd. told The Spectator on behalf of the ownership group in February. Other development partners, the Whitechurch Landowners Group, have filed a similar appeal to advance their site plan for roughly 4,800 homes in an 805-acre urban expansion area on parcels just east of Mount Hope. Consortium representatives didn\'t respond to requests for comment on their OLT appeal. Pothen, of Environmental Defence, figures those appeals "perhaps were placeholders in anticipation" of future provincial changes. The pivot to allow OLT appeals on boundary applications "puts the (tribunal) in charge, effectively," says Don McLean, a representative of Hamilton\'s Stop Sprawl movement. But "opposition to expanding the urban boundary, the opposition to converting farmland, forests and wetlands and so on into somebody\'s private profit, is still there," he added."I don\'t think that\'s changed. I think, if anything, it has probably become more intense."Robichaud said staff expect to present a report to councillors on Bill 185 and other provincial planning changes on May 10.
